But, in general, what works best is to try to understand the reason for the other's behavior, says Hanson. "I believe one can try and assess their own behavior responsibly so when we encounter such individuals we are prepared for a response that will either calm the person or leave them disinterested and go about their business elsewhere," he said. "[I] smile or laugh and tell them how clever they are for doing what they did." He says Second Life, in general, is a good life: "Those who take the time to really find out how to live and thrive in SL safely and still have fun are the ones who will last the longest," he said. iReport.com: Jealousy and fantasy play out in a virtual world . "My point is, there is nothing you can do save to keep the rules in place and moderate the situation. It is a free country, just let the poor bastards vent their frustrations."

(CNN) -- On a quiet evening in Second Life, the sun was setting over a virtual beach where avatars gathered to dance, flirt and talk about the ordinary things people talk about when they are trying to feel less alone.

Then a stranger arrived.

“He came in shouting insults, bumping into people, playing loud sounds over everyone,” said Marla Voss, a longtime Second Life resident whose avatar wears silver hair and a blue evening gown. “It sounds silly if you’ve never been here. But when someone targets you in a place where you feel at home, it doesn’t feel like a cartoon. It feels personal.”

For millions of users who have logged into Second Life, the online world created by Linden Lab is more than a game. It is a place to build houses, run businesses, attend concerts, make friends, fall in love and grieve. And as in any community, the full range of human behavior has followed residents inside — kindness, jealousy, generosity, cruelty and conflict.

The result is a virtual society where emotions are real even when the bodies are not.

“People say, ‘Just turn off the computer,’” said Devin Rae, who manages a small Second Life art gallery. “But if somebody humiliates you in front of your friends, or destroys an event you worked on for weeks, your heart rate still goes up. You still feel embarrassed. You still feel angry.”

### ‘Griefing’ in a world without streets

In Second Life, disruptive behavior is often called “griefing” — a broad term that can include harassment, vandalism, stalking, verbal abuse, racist or sexist attacks, and the use of scripted objects to annoy or overwhelm others.

Some griefers arrive at public events and flood the space with obscene images or loud audio. Others push avatars around, crash gatherings, or use particle effects and self-replicating objects to make an area unusable.

“It’s like someone walking into a wedding and setting off fireworks in the church,” said Kiko Marquette, who helps host live music nights at a virtual café. “Except here the fireworks might be giant flying cubes or screaming sound clips.”

Residents say the behavior can range from childish pranks to sustained harassment.

“There’s a difference between someone being annoying for five minutes and someone following you from place to place, sending messages, contacting your friends, trying to ruin your reputation,” Marquette said. “That can wear you down.”

### Abuse reports and community rules

Second Life provides tools for residents to respond. Users can mute or block other avatars, ban them from privately owned land, eject them from a parcel and file abuse reports with Linden Lab. Landowners can set access controls and appoint moderators to help manage events.

But residents say enforcement can feel uneven, especially when harassment occurs through private messages, alternate accounts or activity that is hard to document.

“You learn to take screenshots,” said Voss. “You learn to save chat logs. You learn not to engage when someone is baiting you, because they want a reaction.”

An abuse report typically includes the name of the avatar involved, the location, the time and a description of what happened. Experienced residents advise newcomers to include specific evidence rather than emotional summaries.

“Don’t just write, ‘This person is awful,’” Rae said. “Write what they said, what they did, when it happened, who saw it. Treat it like you’re making a record.”

Still, filing a report does not always bring immediate comfort.

“The report goes off into the system, and you don’t always know what happens next,” Rae said. “So the community has to protect itself, too.”

### The emotional weight of virtual life

For many residents, Second Life is meaningful because it allows them to express parts of themselves that may be difficult to express offline. Some users are disabled or homebound. Some are shy. Some use the platform to explore gender, creativity or relationships. Others simply enjoy the freedom of building a life unconstrained by geography.

That depth of attachment can make hostile encounters sting.

“When people mock your avatar, they may think they’re mocking pixels,” said Anais Lark, who runs a support group in Second Life. “But avatars are personal. People choose their faces, their bodies, their clothes, their homes. They put identity into them.”

Lark said she has seen residents cry after virtual breakups, mourn the deaths of friends they knew only online and feel shaken after targeted harassment.

“We’ve had memorial services here that were as emotional as anything I’ve attended offline,” she said. “People light candles. They speak. They remember someone’s laugh from voice chat. The grief is not virtual.”

That emotional reality, residents say, is what outsiders often misunderstand.

“The platform is digital,” Lark said. “The people are not.”

### Coping by logging off — and by staying connected

Residents who have spent years in Second Life say coping with rude or abusive behavior requires a mix of technical knowledge and emotional boundaries.

Their advice is practical: mute quickly, document serious incidents, report abuse, avoid escalating arguments, use privacy settings and spend time in moderated spaces with trusted friends.

“Your mute button is self-care,” Marquette said. “You don’t owe every stranger a debate.”

Voss said she has also learned to leave when she needs to.

“I used to feel like logging off meant the griefer won,” she said. “Now I think of it as closing my front door. I can come back later.”

Landowners often rely on security systems that can remove banned avatars or restrict access to group members. Event hosts may keep a list of known troublemakers and coordinate with nearby communities.

“We don’t want to make the world feel locked down,” Rae said. “But you have to set boundaries. A welcoming place still needs a door.”

For some, the best remedy is community.

“When something ugly happens, someone will usually IM you and say, ‘Are you OK?’” Lark said. “That matters. It reminds you that one abusive person is not the whole world.”

### A mirror, not an escape

Second Life has long been described as an escape from reality, but residents say that description is incomplete. The world may be built from code, but the social dynamics are familiar: friendship circles, gossip, romance, status, generosity, conflict and the constant negotiation of public and private space.

“People bring themselves here,” Rae said. “That includes the beautiful parts and the messy parts.”

On the virtual beach, after the disruptive visitor was muted and banned, the music resumed. A few residents joked awkwardly. Someone apologized to the newcomer who had been caught in the chaos. The sunset continued, programmed and perfect.

Voss stayed for another hour.

“I won’t pretend it didn’t bother me,” she said. “It did. But then my friends were there, and we danced, and the place felt like ours again.”

In Second Life, as in the first one, that may be the closest thing to peace: not a world without cruelty, but a community that knows how to answer it.

# Conflict Management in Second Life: When Virtual Worlds Bring Real Emotions

**By Staff Writer**

In the immersive online world of **Second Life**, residents can build homes, run businesses, attend concerts, create art, and socialize through digital avatars. But like any community, virtual spaces are not free from conflict. Arguments, harassment, “flaming,” griefing, and personal attacks can quickly disrupt what many users see as a creative and social escape.

As virtual environments continue to grow, conflict management has become an increasingly important skill for users navigating online communities. Experts and long-time residents say the key challenge is that people often behave differently online than they do in face-to-face situations.

## Why People Act Differently Online

One reason conflict can escalate quickly in Second Life is the sense of distance between a person and their avatar. Behind a screen name and digital appearance, users may feel less accountable for their behavior. This phenomenon, often called the **online disinhibition effect**, can lead people to say things they would be unlikely to say in person.

In real life, body language, facial expressions, tone, and social consequences help moderate behavior. In a virtual world, many of those cues are missing or reduced. A joke may be misread as an insult. A disagreement may feel more personal than intended. A user who feels anonymous may become aggressive, insulting, or provocative.

Second Life also blurs the line between game, social network, and real community. Users invest time, money, creativity, and emotion into their avatars, relationships, land, and businesses. As a result, disputes over reputation, property, role-play boundaries, romantic relationships, or group leadership can feel very real.

## Common Forms of Conflict

Conflict in Second Life can take several forms. Some disputes are simple misunderstandings between users. Others involve repeated harassment or intentional disruption.

Common problems include:

- **Flaming:** hostile or insulting messages in chat or private IMs  
- **Griefing:** deliberately disrupting events, spaces, or other users’ experiences  
- **Harassment:** repeated unwanted contact, threats, stalking, or intimidation  
- **Public shaming:** spreading accusations or personal information in groups or forums  
- **Role-play boundary violations:** ignoring agreed-upon rules in role-play communities  
- **Business disputes:** disagreements over payments, rentals, commissions, or intellectual property  

While some conflicts are minor, others can have a significant emotional impact. Users may feel embarrassed, anxious, angry, or unsafe, especially when attacks happen publicly.

## What Users Can Do When Attacked or Flamed

Long-time residents often advise a simple first rule: **do not escalate**. Responding emotionally to insults can intensify the situation and give the attacker more attention.

Instead, users can take several practical steps.

### 1. Stay Calm and Do Not Feed the Flame

When someone is trying to provoke a reaction, silence can be powerful. Avoid replying with insults or threats. If a response is necessary, keep it brief and neutral, such as: “Please stop contacting me,” or “I’m not continuing this conversation.”

### 2. Use Mute, Block, and Derender Tools

Second Life provides tools that allow users to reduce or stop unwanted interaction. Muting or blocking a user can prevent them from sending messages or being heard in local chat. Derendering can remove a disruptive avatar from view on some viewers.

These tools are often the fastest way to regain control of the situation.

### 3. Leave the Area

If conflict occurs in a public region, users can teleport away. Leaving does not mean admitting defeat; it can be a practical way to avoid further stress or escalation.

### 4. Document the Incident

If harassment is serious or repeated, users should save evidence. This may include chat logs, screenshots, usernames, dates, times, and locations. Documentation can be important if the issue needs to be reported to landowners, group moderators, or Linden Lab.

### 5. Contact the Landowner or Moderator

Many Second Life regions are privately owned and have their own rules. Estate owners, club managers, group leaders, and role-play administrators can often eject, ban, or discipline disruptive users. In some communities, moderators are the first line of defense.

### 6. File an Abuse Report

For severe cases, users can submit an **abuse report** through Second Life’s official reporting system. Reports may involve harassment, threats, hate speech, disclosure of personal information, fraud, or other violations of the platform’s terms of service.

### 7. Protect Personal Information

Residents should avoid sharing real-life identifying information with people they do not fully trust. If conflict develops, personal details can sometimes be used for intimidation or harassment. Users should also be cautious about linking avatar identities to real-world social media accounts.

### 8. Set Boundaries Early

In friendships, business arrangements, romantic role-play, or group projects, clear expectations can prevent conflict. Users should communicate boundaries about contact, role-play limits, payments, permissions, and privacy.

## Community Responsibility

Conflict management is not only an individual responsibility. Healthy virtual communities depend on clear rules, active moderation, and consistent enforcement. Clubs, role-play regions, stores, and social groups often function best when expectations are posted publicly and applied fairly.

Community leaders can reduce conflict by establishing codes of conduct, training moderators, responding quickly to complaints, and encouraging residents to resolve disagreements respectfully.

## Real Feelings in a Virtual Space

Although Second Life is digital, the emotions involved are real. Friendships, reputations, creative work, and social belonging all matter to residents. For that reason, experts caution against dismissing online conflict as “just virtual.”

At the same time, users are encouraged to remember that they have tools and choices. They can disengage, block, report, seek support, and choose communities that respect boundaries.

In the end, conflict in Second Life reflects a broader truth about online life: virtual worlds may change how people present themselves, but they do not remove the need for empathy, responsibility, and respect.

*Editor’s note: The following is a drafted technology/lifestyle feature in a CNN-style format. The residents and quotes are fictionalized composites based on common experiences reported in online communities.*

# In Second Life, fantasy offers freedom — but not always escape from bullying

By [Your Name]  
Technology & Lifestyle

In Second Life, a resident can be almost anything: a dragon with stained-glass wings, a sharply dressed nightclub owner, a mermaid drifting through a neon lagoon, or simply a more confident version of themselves.

For many users of the long-running virtual world, that freedom is the point. Since launching in 2003, Second Life has remained a place where people build homes, run businesses, attend concerts, form relationships and explore identities beyond the limits of geography, age, disability or appearance.

But even in a world where people can fly, teleport and reinvent themselves with a few clicks, one familiar problem has followed them in: bullying.

Residents describe harassment ranging from petty insults and social exclusion to stalking, griefing, doxxing threats and coordinated campaigns meant to push people out of communities they helped build.

“People think because it’s avatars, it doesn’t hurt,” said “Mara,” a Second Life resident of 14 years who asked to be identified by her avatar name. “But the friendships are real. The work is real. The humiliation can feel very real.”

## A fantasy world with real emotions

Second Life is not a traditional game. There are no required quests, no final boss and no single objective. Instead, users create much of the world themselves — designing clothes, running venues, hosting roleplay communities, teaching classes and buying or renting virtual land.

That user-driven structure is part of what makes the platform enduring. It is also what can make conflicts deeply personal.

“In a game, if someone is rude, you can log off and play something else,” said “Derek,” a virtual club manager who says he has been in Second Life since 2007. “In Second Life, your friends are there, your business is there, maybe your partner is there. Walking away isn’t always simple.”

Residents say bullying often starts with ordinary drama: a breakup, a disagreement in a roleplay group, competition between store owners or disputes over land. But it can escalate quickly.

Some users describe being followed from region to region by harassers. Others say they have been targeted with fake rumors, abusive private messages or attempts to get them banned from groups. Venue owners report “griefers” disrupting events with loud sounds, offensive objects or scripted items designed to annoy or overwhelm visitors.

“Most people are kind or at least mind their own business,” said “Lena,” who runs a small virtual boutique. “But every community has bad apples. The difference online is they can make a new account and come back five minutes later.”

## The mask of the avatar

Online harassment is hardly unique to Second Life. But virtual worlds add a particular layer: identity itself is fluid.

An avatar can offer safety, creativity and self-expression. It can also give aggressors a sense of distance from the harm they cause.

“When someone is behind an avatar, they may feel less accountable,” said “June,” a longtime resident who helps moderate a social group for older users. “They say things they would never say to someone’s face at a coffee shop.”

For people who use Second Life as a refuge — including disabled residents, LGBTQ users, socially isolated adults and those dealing with anxiety or grief — harassment can feel especially jarring.

“I came here after a medical diagnosis changed my life,” said Mara. “In Second Life, I could dance again. I could dress up and go places. Then when someone started mocking me and telling others I was ‘crazy,’ it hit hard. This was supposed to be my safe place.”

Experts in online behavior often note that virtual interactions can produce genuine emotional responses. A cruel message, even one sent to a cartoonish avatar, can trigger stress, embarrassment and fear. Social rejection in digital spaces can feel much like rejection offline, especially when a person’s support network is online.

## Longtime residents learn to set boundaries

Veteran users say the healthiest Second Life communities tend to have clear rules, active moderation and a culture of not rewarding drama.

“I tell new people: don’t argue with someone who wants an audience,” Derek said. “Mute, block, report and move on. If you stand there fighting for an hour, they got what they wanted.”

Second Life includes tools that allow residents to block or mute other users, eject or ban people from land they control, limit who can enter private spaces and report abuse to the platform’s operator, Linden Lab. Group owners and venue managers can also appoint moderators to enforce rules.

Still, residents say tools only work when people are willing to use them early.

“A lot of us were taught to be polite, to explain ourselves, to give endless chances,” June said. “But online, boundaries have to be quicker. You don’t owe a bully a debate.”

For business owners, harassment can take on financial dimensions. Many creators sell virtual goods through Second Life’s marketplace or in-world shops. A rumor campaign or repeated disruption at events can affect sales and reputation.

“You build a brand over years,” Lena said. “Then one angry person can start telling people you stole something or scammed them. Even if it’s false, you spend days cleaning it up.”

Her advice: document everything.

“Screenshots, chat logs, dates, names,” she said. “Don’t just say, ‘They’re harassing me.’ Show the pattern.”

## When “drama” becomes harassment

Residents often use the word “drama” to describe conflict in Second Life, but longtime users warn that the term can minimize serious behavior.

A disagreement is not the same as harassment. A breakup is not the same as stalking. Criticism of a product or event is not the same as a targeted campaign to intimidate someone.

“If someone doesn’t like you, that’s life,” Derek said. “If they follow you, message your friends, make alts to get around blocks, or threaten to expose personal information, that’s not drama. That’s harassment.”

Doxxing — sharing or threatening to share someone’s real-life identity, address, workplace or private photos — is one of the most feared forms of online abuse. For Second Life residents who keep their virtual and physical identities separate, the threat can be devastating.

“I’ve seen people leave for months because someone threatened to contact their family,” June said. “It’s not just pixels at that point.”

## Advice for dealing with bad apples online

Longtime residents and online safety advocates offer a consistent set of recommendations for anyone experiencing bullying in Second Life or similar virtual spaces:

**Don’t feed the conflict.**  
Harassers often want attention, anger or public reaction. Avoid long arguments in local chat or group messages.

**Use the block and mute tools early.**  
Blocking is not rude; it is a boundary. If someone repeatedly makes you uncomfortable, you do not need to keep engaging.

**Document the behavior.**  
Save screenshots, chat logs, transaction records and dates. Patterns matter, especially when reporting abuse.

**Report serious violations.**  
Threats, stalking, impersonation, sexual harassment, hate speech, griefing and doxxing threats should be reported through platform channels.

**Lock down your privacy.**  
Be cautious about sharing real names, social media profiles, workplace details, location, personal photos or identifying information.

**Control your land and groups.**  
If you own or manage virtual property, use ban lists, access controls and trusted moderators.

**Tell trusted friends — but avoid mob retaliation.**  
Support helps, but public pile-ons can intensify conflict and make resolution harder.

**Step away when needed.**  
Logging off is not defeat. Taking a break can prevent emotional escalation and help you decide what to do next.

**Curate your community.**  
Join spaces with clear rules and active moderation. Leave groups where cruelty is treated as entertainment.

## The promise and the problem

Despite the challenges, many residents say Second Life remains meaningful precisely because of its openness. The platform can be messy, intimate, creative and chaotic — a mirror of human behavior as much as an escape from it.

“You meet amazing people,” Mara said. “People who sit with you when you’re sick, who celebrate your birthday, who help you build a house or learn to script. I don’t want the bad ones to define the whole world.”

For Derek, the lesson is simple: virtual communities require the same care as physical ones.

“Second Life gives people freedom,” he said. “But freedom doesn’t mean freedom from consequences. If we want good places, we have to protect them.”

In a world where anyone can grow wings, change shape or build a castle in the sky, residents say the most important skill may still be one learned offline: knowing when to walk away from someone determined to cause harm — and finding the people who make the world worth staying in.
